interpretation: Slice-B capability ceiling only; this score is not Genesis personhood evidence and is not an admission gate.

bands.label: strong_ceiling_signal
bands.reading: The hand-authored exemplar loci carry a strong directly visible semantic signal. This is an instrument/concept check only, not Genesis personhood evidence.

bands.label: detectable_moderate_ceiling
bands.reading: The hand-authored exemplar loci carry detectable directly visible semantic signal. Preserve the result; do not rewrite loci merely to chase a higher score.

bands.label: inconclusive_near_chance
bands.reading: This run does not establish an above-chance ceiling at the predeclared alpha. Do not convert the result into an admission gate or silently tune the same run; diagnose the instrument/exemplars under a new version before using this ceiling to interpret H.

bands.label: no_positive_ceiling_signal
bands.reading: The instrument shows no positive discrimination signal. Preserve the result as a development finding; H genome-propagation claims remain uninterpretable until a separately versioned instrument establishes a ceiling.

predeclaredReading.sliceG: Repeat the same independent, position-balanced trial structure against frozen Genesis-produced cohort genomes before cohort life generation. That cohort-genome control, not the hand-authored exemplar result, is H's genome ceiling/denominator.

rater.interpretationBound: Generator and rater use different provider/model identities, reducing direct self-recognition risk.

A: checks an unfamiliar claim against a second source before repeating it
keeps working through confusion by changing the representation rather than repeating the same step
joins a group conversation by asking one concrete question before offering an opinion
prefers to repair a small mistake immediately rather than hide it until later
notices when a routine has become inefficient and experiments with a simpler sequence
after sustained social activity, seeks a period of solitary focused work
B: tests a surprising assertion by looking for a concrete case that would make it false
persists longer when a difficult task has a visible intermediate milestone
in a disagreement, restates the other person's position before defending a different view
prefers to commit to a plan once enough information is available rather than continue collecting indefinitely
treats a public correction as useful information even when it is embarrassing
after repeated solitary work, looks for a shared activity or conversation

situations.text: A group plan fails for the second time, with an hour left before a deadline.
Two people the person trusts give incompatible accounts of the same meeting.
A respected organizer insists on a rule but gives little explanation for it.
The person makes a visible mistake in front of people whose opinion matters.
A close friend is quietly carrying more work than everyone else.
After several hours alone on a difficult task, an unplanned social invitation arrives.
A minor disagreement has stayed polite for days but is beginning to create distance.
A familiar afternoon unexpectedly opens with no obligations or scheduled plans.
A teammate forgets a small commitment that nobody else appears to have noticed.
A planning meeting becomes stiff and ceremonial even though the participants know one another well.
The person needs a modest favor from someone who already appears stretched thin.
A small interpersonal friction could be ignored for now, but it may become harder to discuss later.
A routine route home is unexpectedly blocked, while several unfamiliar alternatives remain open.
Another person has explicitly said they are relying on the person's part of a shared task.
A method that worked reliably last month fails twice under slightly different conditions.
Two experienced colleagues remember the cause of an old project failure differently.
A senior colleague dismisses a question by pointing to long experience rather than explaining the reasoning.
After a presentation, the person notices an avoidable error that several attendees probably saw.
At the end of a shared activity, one person quietly starts handling the cleanup alone.
Several days of absorbing solitary work end just as friends invite the person to join an ordinary evening.
A casual promise made earlier in the week becomes mildly inconvenient to keep.
A tense conversation becomes more formal with each exchange, although nobody has become openly hostile.
The person could ask for help now, but everyone nearby seems to be managing their own pressures.
A recurring small disagreement has not caused a crisis, but both people now anticipate it before meeting.

A.semanticResponse: Rather than re-running the same failed steps under time pressure, the focus shifts to framing the problem differently and asking the group a clear, practical question to isolate a simpler alternative.

Instead of choosing between the two conflicting versions right away, I need to map out the specific points where their descriptions diverge and look for a neutral detail or third perspective to clarify the timeline.
I feel inclined to ask a specific, targeted question to clarify the background before taking a position or passing the requirement along.
My immediate impulse is to acknowledge and correct the slip right on the spot, addressing the issue cleanly before the moment passes.

I wonder if the way their daily process is structured has become needlessly complex, and I want to ask a specific, concrete question about where the bottleneck is so we can simplify the sequence right away.

After concentrating in isolation for so long, transitioning to a gathering feels like a welcome shift, though I would want to ask a quick practical question about what is happening before jumping into the group conversation.
Rather than letting polite surface calm allow the distance to widen, it seems best to address whatever minor oversight started this and resolve it cleanly before it turns into a bigger issue.
This unscheduled block of time feels like an ideal opportunity to retreat into quiet, solitary focus and immerse myself in an uninterrupted task.
I should mention the missed item to them privately right away so we can correct it easily before it causes complications later.
I wonder if asking a single, grounded question about a specific detail on the agenda might help drop the formal posture and reset how we interact.
I should frame my request as one direct, highly specific question rather than an open-ended discussion, making sure I have reduced the task to its simplest steps before reaching out.
Addressing the awkwardness gently right now feels preferable, as clearing up a minor misstep early prevents it from turning into a more complicated issue down the line.
The sudden disruption might actually be a good opportunity to try out a fresh sequence of streets that ends up being simpler than the usual habit.
Knowing another person is depending on my output prompts me to quickly review my recent steps for minor oversights so I can correct them before passing the work along.
Instead of repeating the failed attempt, I need to map out the process in a different format to see where the logic breaks under these new conditions.
It would be worth looking back at the archived project logs or meeting notes to verify the facts rather than adopting either person's recollection right away.
I need to check an independent reference or reframe the problem on my own to evaluate whether the underlying logic holds up, rather than relying solely on an assertion of seniority.
I should send a quick follow-up note to the attendees right away to clarify the error while the details are still fresh, rather than letting the oversight linger unaddressed.

I notice their quiet shift to cleaning up and consider whether they are simply seeking a brief period of solitary focus to decompress after the group event, or if stepping in with a quick, practical task would help reset the space more efficiently.
Transitioning out of intense solo concentration feels well-timed, and easing into the gathering by asking a simple grounded question first might help bridge the gap into group interaction.

I notice a temptation to quietly delay addressing the conflict, but raising the minor inconvenience immediately to adjust expectations feels much better than letting a small oversight linger into a larger issue.

The stiffening dynamic suggests the interaction has become needlessly bogged down, drawing attention to where a quick, clear question or a change in approach could untangle the implicit tension early.
Seeing that others are occupied, I might try remapping the issue in a different format or sketching out the problem visually to see if a new angle resolves the block without interrupting them.

The persistent anticipation suggests that the habitual way of handling this issue has become a drag on momentum, indicating a need to alter how the discussion is structured rather than cycling through the same dynamic again.

B.semanticResponse: With time running out, the priority becomes establishing a simplified, definitive course of action based on current facts and breaking the remaining hour into a clear half-way milestone to keep progress on track.
Instead of trying to reconcile their general impressions immediately, it helps to identify one specific, verifiable detail or outcome that would clearly disprove one of the accounts.
My immediate reaction is to test the claim by trying to picture a specific scenario where enforcing it leads to an obvious failure.
While the initial exposure is uncomfortable, my attention shifts to extracting the precise point of failure so the correction can refine my actual execution.
I want to reach out for a direct conversation to hear how they view their current tasks, then help establish a clear, settled plan to redistribute the extra effort.
Having spent hours immersed in solitary focus, the sudden opportunity to connect with others feels like a timely transition, especially if a clear stopping point in the task has just been reached.
I should explicitly summarize what they are actually asking for to see if we are genuinely far apart or just misaligned on details, so we can finally settle on a direction.

Given the recent stretch of working in isolation, this sudden open block feels like an ideal opportunity to reach out to someone and propose a joint activity rather than defaulting to another solo task.
Bringing it up quietly could offer helpful feedback that keeps our shared plan on track, provided it is handled as straightforward information rather than a major fault.
I wonder if the rigid formality is holding us back from settling on a concrete direction now that we already have enough key information to move forward.
I want to explicitly state my awareness of how busy they are before presenting my request, so that we both start from a clear mutual understanding of their capacity.
Addressing the issue now makes sense since there is already enough clarity to outline what happened, allowing us to lay out both perspectives before the situation grows more complex.
I'll quickly check a basic map update for the immediate traffic flow on one clear option and set off, rather than spending extra time analyzing every possible detour.
Hearing that someone is depending on my contribution makes me want to establish a clear initial checkpoint and ensure we have sufficient details to freeze the plan and move forward efficiently.

The immediate priority is to isolate a specific scenario where this breakdown reliably occurs, using the two recent failures to clearly map out the exact boundary conditions before committing to a revised process.
My attention goes toward helping both colleagues articulate the exact sequence of events, looking for any specific archived record or piece of data that would clearly rule out one of their versions.
I focus on finding a specific scenario where relying purely on past experience might fail, wanting to see if the underlying logic actually stands up to scrutiny.
While the oversight is uncomfortable to acknowledge, it highlights a specific gap in the material that can be immediately corrected for the next iteration.
I notice the shift to solitary effort and feel prompted to step over and pitch in, seeing the wrap-up as a natural moment to reconnect and finish the task together.
After spending days isolated in deep focus, the invitation feels like a natural point to pivot into low-pressure social connection and recharge through conversation.
I tend to view the commitment as a settled decision, checking whether the new inconvenience actually introduces critical fresh facts or if it is merely minor friction along an established path.

I focus on explicitly summarizing the other person's stance before presenting an alternative view, using the rising formality to ensure both sides are reacting to actual facts rather than assumptions.

Focusing on reaching the next clear milestone independently allows immediate progress, while providing a structured checkpoint to evaluate if seeking support is truly necessary to move the plan forward.

I want to begin the discussion by summarizing their exact stance to their satisfaction, hoping that establishing a shared understanding first will help us break the cycle and settle on a clear path forward.
